title: l3-policy-translation-shadow-investigation-2026-03-12
content:
Summary:

This note documents the investigation into an on-prem customer incident where L3 network policy translations generated overlapping iptables rules that shadowed expected accept rules, causing sporadic control-plane RPC failures and customer firewall resets. Impact was confined to one customer deployment (edge cluster in EU-west region) but exposed a translation edge-case in the policy compiler that we need to address before broad Dedicated/Private rollouts.

Key findings (TL;DR):
- A translation bug in our L3 policy compiler produced an iptables rule ordering that allowed a broad DNAT/masquerade jump rule to appear before a more specific accept rule. This resulted in packets hitting the broad rule first and being NATed/mapped in ways that mismatched the customer's stateful firewall expectations (asymmetric NAT), leading to TCP resets and failed control-plane handshakes.
- The issue surfaced only for a specific combination: policies with overlapping /24 CIDRs plus hostEndpoint-like exceptions (host-level sockets). The translator used a heuristic that sorted by CIDR size but did not account for exceptions, causing 'shadowing' ordering.
- Short-term mitigation was a config rollback for the affected customer's policy and enabling a supplemental conntrack rule on the node to tolerate early NAT translations. Long-term fix: change compiler ordering, add unit/integration tests, and update on-prem runbook.

Impact:
- Time window: 2026-03-11 22:14 UTC -> 2026-03-12 03:05 UTC (customer reported spike in control-plane gRPC timeouts and occasional application TCP resets).
- Affected components: on-prem node network stack (iptables/ipvs layer), Redwood Private controlplane RPCs from customer agents, customer perimeter firewall (stateful).
- Customer-visible: 2–3% increased 5xx on control-plane dependent endpoints, several agent reconnects, transient partial availability for a small set of pods behind service mesh. No data loss reported; logs show failed initial handshakes and TCP RSTs.

Timeline (concise):
- 2026-03-11 22:14 UTC: Customer SRE Slack -> reported "intermittent agent disconnects and resets".
- 2026-03-11 22:22 UTC: Eng oncall (Daniel) triaged; observed burst of SYN/ACK retries and RSTs in kube-proxy logs.
- 2026-03-11 22:40 UTC: Captured iptables-save and conntrack entries from affected node.
- 2026-03-11 23:05 UTC: Recreated policy locally with same inputs; reproduced overlapping rule ordering.
- 2026-03-12 00:10 UTC: Deployed temporary revert of client policy delta (customer approval).
- 2026-03-12 01:00 UTC: Enabled conntrack-permissive rule on node (workaround) to allow control-plane backfill connections.
- 2026-03-12 03:05 UTC: Customer reports stabilization; monitoring shows errors return to baseline.

Evidence (excerpts):
- iptables-save snippet (anonymized):
  -A REDWOOD-FORWARD -s 10.20.0.0/24 -j MASQUERADE
  -A REDWOOD-FORWARD -s 10.20.0.12/32 -j ACCEPT

  Notice MASQUERADE appears before the specific accept for 10.20.0.12 which allows earlier DNAT/NAT to alter tuple before accept check.

- conntrack dump (relevant lines):
  tcp 6 120 ESTABLISHED src=10.20.0.12 dst=198.51.100.42 sport=42022 dport=443 packets=12 bytes=840 src=198.51.100.42 dst=203.0.113.10 sport=443 dport=42022 packets=10 bytes=792 [ASSURED] mark=0 use=1

  Observed entries where src/dst sides did not match customer's firewall expectations, so firewall dropped follow-up packets and triggered RSTs.

Root cause hypothesis and mechanics:
- The policy compiler sorts rules by CIDR prefix length but treats host-exception rules differently. When a policy contains a host-scoped allow (x/32) plus a broader network allow or masquerade, an internal translation path attempted to merge rules for efficiency and emitted a MASQUERADE jump rule early. For certain kernel versions and with upstream NAT/mangle orderings, that MASQUERADE rewrote packet tuples before later ACCEPT rules could be evaluated, causing state mismatch with customer firewall.
- Customer firewall is stateful and binds state to 5-tuple seen at perimeter. Early NAT changes made the first packet seen by firewall differ from later packets causing it to drop or reset.

Temporary mitigation applied:
- Reverted the specific policy delta that introduced the overlapping CIDRs. (Change id: SREP-4123-revert-2)
- Applied a node-level conntrack tolerance rule (audit-only -> permissive) to allow connections with slight tuple drift for a short TTL. Implementation command used on affected nodes: 
  sudo sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established=14400
  (Note: this increases established timeout — used only as a short-term tolerance knob)
- Coordinated with customer to temporarily open a perimeter rule to accept the NATed tuple until rollback completed.

Permanent fixes and engineering actions (owners assigned):
- Compiler patch: update rule ordering algorithm to never place MASQUERADE/DNAT jumps ahead of more specific host-level ACCEPTs. Add explicit ordering constraints. Owner: Sven. ETA: 2026-03-20. (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/private-deploy/pull/278)
- Add integration tests: emulate overlapping CIDR+host-exception cases across supported kernel versions (5.4, 5.15, 6.x). Owner: Priya. ETA: 2026-03-18.
- Add e2e test in CI that runs iptables-save for policy inputs and asserts no MASQUERADE rules precede specific ACCEPT rules for identical families. Owner: Daniel. ETA: 2026-03-22.
- Monitoring: add rule-level translation alerts (classifier) so that when a compiler emits an ordering that could shadow, we flag it at deploy time. Owner: eng-observability. ETA: 2026-03-30.

Runbook updates (immediate changes):
- Create a new runbook section "policy-shadowing" under private-deploy runbooks with the following steps:
  1) Collection: grab iptables-save, nft list ruleset (if using nft), conntrack -L, and /var/log/redwood/agent.log from affected node.
  2) Quick diagnostic: grep for MASQUERADE/DNAT lines and check for identical CIDR collisions with host exceptions. Command: iptables-save | sed -n '/MASQUERADE/,/ACCEPT/p' 
  3) Mitigation order: if safe, revert policy delta OR apply a temporary conntrack tolerance knob (see mitigation above).
  4) Customer coordination checklist: request perimeter short-term temporary accept of NATed tuple and notify of expected window.
  5) Escalation: if rollback is not possible and packet loss >10% for >30m, escalate to SRE lead and on-call network infra.

Operational notes and alternatives considered:
- We debated automating a live reordering on the node via a controlplane agent patch that re-applies iptables ordering. Rejected as risky: live reordering can drop established connections and cause more customer-visible resets.
- We considered hard-disabling masquerade in the translator; this is not safe generally because some topologies depend on MASQUERADE for egress. So the correct fix is ordering + better policy analysis.

Post-incident follow-ups (owners + dates):
- Sven: submit compiler patch + unit tests. Due 2026-03-20.
- Priya: integration matrix and kernel-version test harness. Due 2026-03-18.
- Daniel: add e2e CI assertion and a deploy-time warning if potential shadowing detected. Due 2026-03-22.
- Aisha: update on-prem runbook "policy-shadowing" and circulate for review. Due 2026-03-15.
- CS/SE: ensure customer-facing recap and change log is delivered by 2026-03-14.

Open questions and risks:
- Are there other translation heuristics that merge rules across families (IPv6 vs IPv4) that could cause similar ordering issues? (Action: include IPv6 cases in integration tests.)
- Should we introduce a linter in the console UI to warn customers when they create overlapping CIDR + host exceptions? (UX + product question; loop in product-hosted-api).
- Long-term: consider formal proof or model checker for policy compiler ordering invariants.

Appendix (commands & artifacts collected):
- iptables-save output (redacted) attached in linked artifacts (SREP-4123-iptables-dump-03-11).
- conntrack dump captured to S3: s3://redwood-incident-evidence/4123/conntrack-03-11.log
- Repro script used by eng (repro-policy.sh) attached to PR.

Notes to on-call and future readers:
- If you hit a similar SES (sporadic escalation) from a customer behind a stateful perimeter, look for early NAT/masquerade rules in the compiled output before going deeper into packet captures. That anomaly is a telltale sign for this class of bug.
- Keep customer communication tight: most customers accepted the short rollback because the change was a small policy delta. Have the rollback playbook handy in the private-deploy console.

Document history:
- 2026-03-12: initial investigation notes (Aisha, Daniel).
- 2026-03-13: added compilation hypothesis and assigned owners (Sven, Priya), updated with PR link and CI tasks.

End of file.
